A contractor whose client asked them to install the Drata agent on their own machine said they felt strongly against running an agent on their machine. Their strategy so far was to ignore the request, and they said quitting was the most appealing option if forced.

A commenter said ignoring the Drata request won't make it go away. If you're in the company's corporate directory, you show up as noncompliant in the Drata dashboard. They said running such an agent is extremely normal on company hardware used for business.

The contractor argued the Drata requirement came from sales wanting to show prospects a 'SOC 2 Audited' certificate, not from real security concerns, and said the requirement doesn't offer much actual security.

Suggested workaround for the Drata agent: only install it on a company-owned laptop dedicated to that client. Or lease a dedicated laptop and pass the monthly cost on in your invoice, rather than running it on personal hardware shared with other clients.

The contractor listed ways to isolate the Drata agent: run it in a VM, use an old laptop with the Wi-Fi card removed, or use a dedicated machine on a separate VLAN routed through a VPN. Their client agreed to pay for a new laptop.
Another commenter warned that installing the agent in a VM may not hide anything, since it's trivial for software to detect a VM and a competent agent would report that back.
